title: When It Breaks
blocks: Dr. Okafor signed with a fountain pen.

It was the third of February, a Tuesday, in her office at the clinic, at a desk that had been cleared for the occasion by sweeping everything on it into a drawer. The contract was a single page. Priya had written it, in plain sentences, with a number in the middle of it. It said that Loopback would check in each morning with the patients the clinic chose, and tell the person each patient had named if a patient went quiet; that the clinic would pay two hundred dollars a month; and that either side could stop whenever it liked, for any reason, by saying so.

"I've signed things that were thirty pages long," said Dr. Okafor, "and understood none of them and been robbed by all of them." She uncapped the pen. "This one I understand. It's a pity. I feel I'm cheating."

It was the first money anyone had ever paid Loopback. I'd expected a rush. What I felt was the small, specific weight of something I'd have to keep doing. She gave the pen a little shake, signed in a looping hand that took up three lines, and slid the page across the desk, and said, "Now. I'll tell you what I told you in October."
"Come back in flu season," I said.

"It's February." She looked over her glasses at me. "This is flu season. I'm going to put the rest of my discharges on this before the end of the month, the ones I can't reach on Sundays, and if it breaks I'm going to find out before you do." She capped the pen. "I'm not saying that to frighten you. I'm saying it because that's when a thing is actually a thing. It should make my Tuesday easier. If it doesn't, I'll tell you on Wednesday."
It was Maya's test, in a different mouth: *does it make somebody's Tuesday easier?* I'd never heard anyone else say it.
"Because that's the day I can't find anyone," said Dr. Okafor. "Nobody ever breaks a leg on a Tuesday. They break it on a Saturday, and then on Tuesday nobody has called them back."

It was a Thursday, in the middle of the worst flu month in six years, and I was on the phone with Maya, which by then was a habit. We'd started in January, without discussing it: at about eleven each night, she called me, from her couch or her bed, and we talked for some number of minutes about nothing in particular, and then one of us said *okay* in a particular way and hung up. That night we were at twelve minutes. She was telling me about a woman who'd come into the pharmacy with a prescription in a language Suresh read but couldn't pronounce, and I was sitting on my bed with the laptop open, looking at a dashboard I'd promised Priya I'd stop watching, when the third cheap phone on my desk began to ring.

I should explain the third cheap phone. It was the last of the demo phones from the waiting room, the one with the crack across the screen, and since December I'd bought it a SIM card and put its number at the bottom of every check-in text, in gray, with no name, in a fit of something I couldn't name: *Something wrong? Call this number.* Priya had insisted on the separate phone. ("If it's going to ring at three in the morning, it doesn't ring on your real one.") In two months it had rung nine times, and eight were the same man in Milpitas, who wanted to know if Ruben's was open on Sundays and had decided I was the person to ask.
"Is that the crack phone?" said Maya.
"Put me on speaker," she said. "I'm not going anywhere."
I hadn't thought about it. I put her on speaker, and carried both phones and the laptop into the kitchen, because the table was bigger, and picked up the crack one.

"Is this the number on the text?" A woman's voice, high, controlled, like a cup that was being held level on a moving train. "It says my mother hasn't answered her check-in. It's eleven o'clock at night."

I looked at the dashboard. I felt it happen. It's hard to describe the feeling of reading a number you've known your whole working life and seeing it have an entirely different meaning: the little column that said **NOT ANSWERED** had fifty-eight names in it, every one of them red, and the little column that said **PERSONS NOTIFIED** had fifty-eight beside it, and the time at the top of the screen said 11:07 p.m.
"I'm going to find out," I said. "Hold on. One minute. Please tell me your mother's name."
She told me. I looked her up. She'd answered at 6:04 that morning. She was one of Dr. Okafor's first ones, and she had answered every morning since.
"She did answer," I said. "She answered at 6:04 this morning. The message you got was wrong. It was our mistake. I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. Is she there?"
"She's—" The voice did a thing. "I don't know. I'm in Modesto. I'm getting in the car."
"Don't get in the car," I said. "Please. Call her. If she doesn't pick up in five minutes, call me back, and I'll—" I didn't know what. "I'll stay on the phone."
A message lit up the laptop. It was Priya: *I see it. Coming.* The crack phone rang again in my hand before I'd hung up the first call.
"Keep going," said Maya, from the table. "I'll stay on."
What had happened was an embarrassingly small thing, and the small ones are the ones I trust now.

That afternoon, Priya had moved us to a new computer. A bigger one, in a room somewhere, for the flu-season load. It was her job, and she'd done it carefully, and she'd checked everything she knew to check. What she hadn't known, because no one had told her and it wasn't something you'd think to ask, was that the new computer believed it was in a different place. It kept its clock eight hours from where we were. Its seven in the morning, the moment each day when the system says *nobody's answered yet; tell their person,* was our eleven at night.

So at 11:05 p.m., on a Thursday, in February, the new computer looked at fifty-eight people who had not yet been asked how they were, and decided that every one of them had gone quiet, skipped the asking, and went straight to the telling. It even sent each patient her own note, *we told your person,* which most of them had silenced or slept through. That was the only part that worked as designed.
That's it. A clock in the wrong country.

Priya arrived at 11:40 in an Uber, because she'd been too shaky to drive and would never have admitted it, in flannel pajama pants and her husband's parka, with her laptop in a canvas bag and a face like a locked door. She didn't say hello. She came in and sat at the kitchen table and opened the machine, and I went on talking to a man in Fresno about his wife.

Kyle came out of his room at 11:55 in a T-shirt that said something about a marathon he hadn't run. He stood in the hallway and looked at the two of us, at the crack phone, at the mixing bowl on the counter, and at Maya's voice, coming through the speaker on the table, saying, quietly, *It's all right. Keep going.*
"Make tea," said Priya, without looking up.
"Second person reporting for duty," said Kyle to the room, and went to the kettle.

She had it fixed at 12:06. It took twenty-six minutes. I watched her do it, between calls, in glances: her shoulders square, her hands still, her face lit from below like a person reading a map in a cave. At 12:06 she said, "That's the clock," quietly. At 12:10 she said, "And now I'm sending the apology." I asked her what it said, and she turned the laptop around.
Tonight's message about [name] was our mistake, not theirs. They are fine. We are sorry. If you'd like to talk, call Nate, any time, at the number below.
"It's true," said Priya. "You'll be awake anyway."
There were thirty-four calls, and I answered all of them.

I kept a tally on the back of an envelope, in pencil, in strokes. I could tell you what they said, but I'd rather tell you who they were. A man in Fresno. A teenager, who said *I'm the person on my grandma's thing, did it say she's okay,* in a voice that cracked on the last word, and whom I told, *yes, she's okay, she's fine, you did everything right.* A woman from the county who'd been at a dinner and said, *I don't know what to do with a wrong message that sounds so right.* A man who began, when I said *this is Nate,* with "Oh. A person," in a voice from which something had gone, and then shouted anyway, for four minutes, about his mother, about the ambulance he'd nearly called, and then, without any change in his voice, said *I'm sorry, I'm not shouting at you, I've been awake since five,* and I said *you're allowed.* By the end of the night, eight of them had said some version of *Oh. A person.*

An old woman, who was a patient, and who had answered the phone when her son called her, and who had then called the number at the bottom of the text, herself, on her own telephone, to say, with enormous clarity, "Young man, I'm right here. I'm watching Jeopardy. Somebody sent my son a message that said I hadn't answered. I haven't *been* asked. Do you know the category? It's Potent Potables. I'd like to be left alone." I apologized to her for eleven minutes. She stayed on for the whole thing. At the end she said, "You sound tired," and hung up.

Each time, I said the same thing. I hadn't decided to. It came out on the third call and stayed: *This was our mistake. It wasn't yours. They're fine. I'm sorry. What would help?* I said it in my own voice, without a script, and I noticed somewhere around the twentieth call that it wasn't a technique. It was only true.
At ten to one, there was a silence on the table, and a voice that wasn't on the crack phone said, quietly, from the speaker: "You're saying the same thing to everyone."

"No." It was Maya, in her bed, in the dark, with her voice low. "It's good. It's only that I've heard it before. It's what my mother says when a prescription is wrong." She paused. "She says it in Tamil. The last part is always *What do you need?*"
I wrote it on the envelope. Under the tally. I didn't write it so I'd remember. I wrote it so my hands would be doing something.
The last call came at 2:10, and it was Dr. Okafor.

"I've had eight families call me since midnight," she said, in a voice that I swear was awake, upright, and in a cardigan. "All of them said a young man picked up. All of them. I've had a dozen vendors in twenty years. I have never once had one pick up." There was a pause. "Are you fixing it?"
"Good. I'm not canceling. I'd like a report on Tuesday." The line was quiet for a moment. "Tell your co-founder I said she has a good clock."

"I called once at seven past midnight, and you picked up, and a woman in the background said *that's the clock,*" said Dr. Okafor. "I've been a doctor for twenty-six years. I listen to the background." She hung up.
Priya was at the table with her hands around a mug that Kyle had put there, which she had not touched. She was looking at the screen, at the little column that now said **NOT ANSWERED: 0.**
"It was mine," she said. "I moved the server. I didn't check the clock. It's a thing you check."

"I put a phone number on the text," I said. "If I hadn't, it would have rung nowhere, and nobody would have found out until morning, and dozens of people would have lain awake thinking someone was dead." I sat down across from her. "You built it so that a person finds out. I built it so that a person picks up. That's two jobs. It was the company's night."
She looked at me for a long time. Then she picked up the tea, and drank some of it, and made a face.
"It's the best cold tea I've ever had." She put her head down on her folded arms, on the table, next to the laptop, and said into her sleeve, "Don't tell anyone I did this."
I picked up the crack phone. I put it in a drawer, face down, where it couldn't ring unobserved, and sat with her until her Uber came.
My own phone was still face up on the table, where I'd left it, with the speaker open, and the little timer on it said 3 hours, 41 minutes.
"Yes," said Maya, in the dark, in a voice with no edges left on it. "I didn't want to hang up until you'd finished." There was a pause. "Good night, Nate."
She didn't hang up. I could hear her breathing for a little while. Then the line went quiet, and then, a minute later, it clicked.

It was a Saturday at the pharmacy. There was a line of nine, and a man arguing politely with Suresh about the price of something, and Lakshmi at the register. I'd brought the tins. She weighed them in her hands, which she does, and set them next to the receipt roll, and did not look at me.

She said it to Maya. (Maya had told them on Friday. I hadn't known she'd told anyone.) Maya was stocking something, at the far end of the counter, with her coat on the hook and her sleeves rolled. She didn't turn around.

Lakshmi put down the tins. She took a pencil from behind her ear. Behind her, on the wall, on the strip of receipt paper held up with a thumbtack, I saw the bottom line of the column, where it said, in her small upright hand, *Nate. Cup. Sat.* The pencil moved. I couldn't see what she wrote. I saw the back of her hand, and the pencil's little flick at the end, crossing a *t.*

"Hm," said Lakshmi. She put the pencil behind her ear. She turned her head, at last, and looked at me, with the expression I'd been trying to read for three months, which I finally understood was only *attention.* "You ate?"
"I had a bagel and a banana."
"That," said Lakshmi, "is still a no," and she handed me a steel tin.
It was the following Wednesday that Maya's car died on the 101.

It was ten to one in the morning, on the shoulder, south of the airport, in the stretch where the freeway runs flat and lit and lonely between two hills that aren't there. She'd been at the store doing the inventory, which her parents had asked her to do, because the family does the work, and because the wholesaler's delivery was due Thursday. I was in bed in Mountain View, and my phone buzzed on the nightstand, and I picked it up at the first ring. I've thought since about why, and what I think is this: that I'd had thirty-four calls, and I'd learned what it does to a person when the phone is answered.
"Hi," said Maya. "I'm not calling to be fixed."

"On the 101. Near the airport. It just stopped. It made a noise like a cough." She was standing on the shoulder. I could hear the trucks. "I've called the roadside people. They said ninety minutes. I'm fine. I'm calling because I didn't want to sit here alone with a dead car, and I didn't want to call my parents and have my mother wake my father. I'm not asking you to come."
"It's thirty if I speed a little."
"Stay on the phone," I said, and I heard my voice catch, and I put on the closest pair of pants.

She stayed on the phone. I drove with it on the dash, and she told me, in a low, dry voice, about a patient who'd asked whether the pharmacy could put the pills in an envelope shaped like a heart, for his wife, who was in the hospital, and I said yes, and she said *I know you don't know that,* and I said *I'm learning,* and she didn't answer. At one point, somewhere near Burlingame, she said, without any warning, "I called you first. Before my father. Before Jules." She let the trucks go by. "I want you to know that I noticed."
"That's a Nate thing to say." But her voice had changed.

She was on the shoulder when I got there, in her coat, sitting on the guardrail with her feet up on a piece of concrete, waiting for a bus in a bad neighborhood. I pulled up behind her car with my hazards on. I got out. I didn't say anything. I sat down next to her, on the guardrail, and the rail was cold through my pants.
She looked at me. She looked at my feet, and then up.

"One's a loafer." She started to laugh. She put the heel of her hand to her mouth and laughed, silently, the way you laugh when you've been holding something carefully for a long time, and then she was crying, briefly, without sound, with her shoulders, and I didn't say a word. I didn't say *it's okay.* I didn't say *you don't have to.* It wasn't wisdom. It was only that I'd used up every other sentence, at a kitchen table, with a man from Fresno.
I put my arm around her. It was a clumsy thing, on a guardrail, in the wind of passing trucks. She let me.
The tow truck came at ten to two. It turned out to be forty minutes early, which a person at the roadside company would later say was a first.
note:
At work, when something breaks:
*1. Pick up.*
*2. This was our mistake. It wasn't yours.*
*3. They're fine. I'm sorry.*
*4. What would help?*

At home, when Maya calls late:
*1. Pick up on the first ring.*
*2. Where are you?*
*3. Stay on the phone.*
*4. Find two shoes. They don't have to match.*

Thirty-four calls, tallied on the back of an envelope, taught me the work script. Eight people said some version of *Oh. A person.* Nobody remembered the clock being wrong. They remembered a voice at midnight. Maya taught me the home one from the shoulder of the 101, when she said she wasn't calling to be fixed. So: don't say *it's okay.* Don't say *you don't have to.* Don't ask what I can do. Say I'm coming.
